subject: Polity
description: Covers Ordinary bills, Money bills, Speaker authority.

questions.stem: According to the Indian Constitution, an ordinary bill can originate in:

options.option_text: Either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha
Only the Lok Sabha
Only the Rajya Sabha
A joint sitting of both Houses

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: An ordinary bill (a bill that is not a Money Bill, Financial Bill, or Constitutional Amendment Bill) can be introduced in either House of Parliament—the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. It can be introduced by a minister (Public Bill) or by any other member (Private Member's Bill). 
DECOY BUSTING: Money Bills (Article 110) are an exception; they can ONLY be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and that too only on the prior recommendation of the President. 
EXAM INSIGHT: If an ordinary bill passed by one House is rejected by the other House, or if the houses disagree on amendments for more than six months, a deadlock is reached. The President can summon a joint sitting of both Houses (under Article 108) to resolve it, which is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: In the context of the Indian Parliament, who holds the final authority to decide whether a particular bill is a 'Money Bill' or not?

options.option_text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The President of India
The Prime Minister of India
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 110(3) of the Constitution explicitly states that if any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha shall be FINAL. When a Money Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha and when it is presented to the President for assent, it is endorsed with the certificate of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha signed by him that it is a Money Bill.
DECOY BUSTING: The President recommends the introduction of a Money Bill, but does not certify it. The Rajya Sabha has virtually no power over a Money Bill (it can only delay it for 14 days or make non-binding recommendations).
EXAM INSIGHT: This power of the Speaker was highly debated when the government controversially passed the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill in 2016 to bypass the Rajya Sabha (where the ruling party lacked a majority). The Supreme Court upheld the Speaker's decision, though a dissenting judge disagreed.

questions.stem: Under Article 108 of the Constitution, a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve a deadlock CANNOT be convened for which of the following?

options.option_text: Ordinary Bills pending in Rajya Sabha for over six months
Money Bills, which follow a separate constitutional procedure
Constitutional Amendment Bills needing a Presidential recommendation
Private Member's Bills rejected by Rajya Sabha after Lok Sabha passage

questions.explanation: Article 108(1) permits joint sitting only for ordinary Bills when Rajya Sabha rejects, indefinitely delays, or disagrees on amendments. Money Bills are governed by Article 109, which gives Rajya Sabha only 14 days and no veto — Lok Sabha's will prevails unconditionally with no provision for joint sitting. Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368 similarly cannot be resolved via joint sitting. Option C is wrong because Presidential recommendation is a separate requirement, not a bar on joint sitting.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes 'Zero Hour' in the Indian Parliament?

options.option_text: The first hour of each sitting, formally reserved for Question Hour
An informal period beginning at noon for raising urgent public importance matters
Time allocated every Friday specifically for Private Member's Bills debates
A post-adjournment session where supplementary questions may be raised by MPs

questions.explanation: Zero Hour is not mentioned in the Constitution or the Rules of Procedure — it is a parliamentary convention that evolved in the 1960s. It begins immediately after Question Hour ends (around 12 noon) and allows members to raise matters of urgent public importance without prior notice. Option A describes Question Hour itself. Friday sittings for Private Member's Bills are a formal Rules-based arrangement distinct from Zero Hour. Post-adjournment supplementary questions are not a recognised procedure.

questions.stem: Which type of Cut Motion, if passed in Lok Sabha during demands for grants, reduces the amount of a particular demand to Re. 1, signalling wholesale disapproval of the policy underlying that demand?

options.option_text: Token Cut Motion, used to raise a specific grievance on the subject of demand
Economy Cut Motion, specifying a reduced sum to be voted for the demand
Policy Cut Motion, signalling rejection of the underlying policy of demand
Censure Cut Motion, symbolically censuring the ministry's financial approach

questions.explanation: A Policy Cut Motion demands reduction to Re. 1, expressing that the House disapproves of the policy behind the demand. An Economy Cut Motion (Option B) demands reduction by a specified sum, suggesting a specific saving in expenditure. A Token Cut Motion (Option A) demands reduction by Rs. 100 and is used to ventilate a specific grievance against administration. 'Censure Cut Motion' (Option D) is not a recognised parliamentary procedure — candidates who conflate 'censure motion' with cut motions are a common examiner target.

questions.stem: A Bill that contains provisions both for imposition of a new tax (qualifying under Article 110) and other non-financial matters, introduced exclusively in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation, is classified as:

options.option_text: A Money Bill under Article 110, requiring only Lok Sabha's final passage
Financial Bill (Category I) under Article 117(1): Rajya Sabha may suggest amendments
Financial Bill (Category II) under Article 117(3), which can originate in Rajya Sabha
An Ordinary Bill with financial implications, resolvable through a joint sitting

questions.explanation: A Financial Bill (Category I) under Article 117(1) contains money-bill provisions plus other matters. Unlike a Money Bill, Rajya Sabha is not reduced to a 14-day rubber stamp — it can suggest amendments (though Lok Sabha need not accept them). A Money Bill (Option A) contains ONLY the specified financial matters and Rajya Sabha has no amendment power. A Financial Bill (Category II) under Article 117(3) has no money-bill provisions at all but involves Consolidated Fund expenditure and can originate in either House — the opposite of the scenario described.

questions.stem: Under Article 249, when Rajya Sabha passes a special majority resolution empowering Parliament to legislate on a State List subject, for how long does the resolution remain in force before it lapses?

options.option_text: Six months, but renewable indefinitely by subsequent Rajya Sabha resolutions
One year, extendable by further Rajya Sabha resolutions of one year each time
Two years, after which it automatically lapses with no possibility of extension
Three years, coinciding with one full term of the Rajya Sabha membership

questions.explanation: Article 249(2) specifies that the resolution remains in force for one year from the date of passing, and may be extended by successive resolutions of one year each. Option A (six months) is a common trap — six months is actually the post-expiry grace period during which a law already made under Article 249 continues to operate under Article 249(3), not the duration of the resolution itself. Options C and D have no constitutional basis.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Censure Motion from a No-Confidence Motion in Lok Sabha practice?

options.option_text: Censure requires 50 members' support to be admitted; No-Confidence requires 100 members
Censure targets specific ministers with reasons; No-Confidence covers whole ministry
Censure is movable only in Rajya Sabha; No-Confidence is exclusive to Lok Sabha
If Censure passes, the government resigns; a failed No-Confidence dissolves Parliament

questions.explanation: A Censure Motion targets a specific minister or group of ministers and must specify reasons; even if passed, it does not constitutionally compel resignation. A No-Confidence Motion is directed at the entire Council of Ministers, need not state reasons, and if passed requires the whole government to resign under Article 75(3). Option A reverses the numbers — it is No-Confidence that requires at least 50 members under Rule 198; there is no such threshold for Censure. Option C is wrong — both motions are moved in Lok Sabha. Option D inverts consequences: No-Confidence (not Censure) triggers resignation.

questions.stem: Amendment to which of the following provisions does NOT require ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2)?

options.option_text: Article 54, which provides for the manner of election of the President
Any List in the Seventh Schedule — Union, State, and Concurrent Lists
Article 368 itself, which governs the procedure for amending the Constitution
Article 148, on appointment and tenure of the Comptroller and Auditor General

questions.explanation: The proviso to Article 368(2) enumerates provisions requiring state ratification: Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, 241; Chapter IV of Part V (Supreme Court, Articles 124–147); Chapter V of Part VI (High Courts); Chapter I of Part XI (legislative relations); the Seventh Schedule Lists; representation of States in Parliament; and Article 368 itself. Article 148 (CAG) falls in Chapter V of Part V — which is NOT in the enumerated list. The most tempting wrong answer is Option C, as students know Article 368 requires special majority but may not know it also needs state ratification. The examiners exploit confusion between 'Chapter IV of Part V' (Supreme Court) and 'Chapter V of Part V' (CAG).
